fig1_debye_entropy.svg: The third law needs the heat capacity to die at the origin, and it does. With the low-temperature Debye form $c_p=aT^3$ (debye_cp) the entropy integrand $c_p/T=aT^2$ also vanishes, so $S(T)=\int_0^Tc_p/T'\,dT'=aT^3/3$ converges to a finite value and can be anchored at $S(0)=0$ for a pure crystalline solid (standard_entropy_at_zero). The circles are the module's numerical quadrature absolute_entropy, which lands on the closed form absolute_entropy_debye. Had $c_p$ stayed finite at $T=0$, the integral would diverge logarithmically and absolute entropies would not exist.
fig2_unattainability.svg: The practical face of the third law. Even a perfectly reversible refrigerator has COP $\beta_{max}=T_C/(T_H-T_C)$ (carnot_cop_refrigerator), so removing one joule from a body at $T_C$ costs $(T_H-T_C)/T_C$ joules of work. Against a 300 K room that is 2 J at 100 K, 29 J at 10 K and 299 J at 1 K — the cost diverges as $T_C\to0$. Absolute zero is not merely hard to reach; reaching it in a finite number of steps is impossible, which is the unattainability statement of the third law.
